utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, you may commence your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Hayman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Watkins.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we begin with a short statement by you of your background, your education, and your military experience in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My education, after completing secondary school, I studied a degree in economics and politics at Leeds and then subsequently took a master's degree at the London School of Economics. After a short period when I was farming on the family farm, I joined Her Majesty's forces and served as an officer after training at Sandhurst for eight years in the British army in the Royal Horse Artillery, and left with the substantive rank of captain but in a local capacity the rank of major. I served for eight years. I was then recruited by the Foreign and Commonwealth Office and seconded to the European Community Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you actually serve as a European Community monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I served for a total of two years. I was recruited in January of 1993, but actually went to the Balkans in February 1993, and after a short induction at Zagreb, I went to -- I was posted to Bosnia, where I started as a monitor in Tomislavgrad, and I then became the head of the coordination centre in Travnik in about May or June of 1993, and I stayed in that position until the middle of October 1993, when I was transferred to Mostar as the head of the coordination centre in Mostar. And I was in Mostar until February 1994. I then had to return to the United Kingdom and was back in UK for three months. And in, I think, the end of April 1994 came back to the ECMM and served for a short while as a monitor in Karlovac, and then was quickly appointed to become the head of the coordination centre in Topusko. After some months in that position I was appointed as the head of the regional centre in Zenica with responsibility for all of the monitoring mission in Bosnia and I went to Zenica, where the headquarters was, and stayed there from August 1994 through to February 1995, a six-month period. After that, I went to Zagreb and I served in the headquarters as one of the advisors to the ambassador, the head of the mission. And I finally left the European Community Monitoring Mission in April 1995, and then after a short break I worked for the United Nations in Zagreb with the SRSG, Yasushi Akashi, as a political advisor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then is it fair to say the period that you were on the ground in Central Bosnia observing events, meeting the relevant officials, was first as head of the CC Travnik from roughly June to October of 1993, and then as head of RC Zenica from roughly August 1994 until February of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's true, although, of course, when I was a monitor in Tomislavgrad, I did a lot of work in Gornji Vakuf, and that is of course Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very good. During these tours of duty, did you have occasion to meet with the appellant, Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, was that on two or three occasions or on many more occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the time I was the head of the CC Travnik, I was meeting Colonel Blaskic probably two, three times a week, and then as the head of the regional centre, by then, Colonel Blaskic had been promoted to General Blaskic and was operating in the Posusje headquarters down in Herzegovina, and I met him on probably three or four occasions, certainly not as many as in Central Bosnia, but I continued contact because of his senior position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your meetings with him over these time periods more of a social type or were they working meetings with substantive agendas and follow-up action on these various agenda items?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They weren't really social. There wasn't much time for social activity. It was certainly one-to-one meetings and also meetings where there was a gathering of several leaders in which I would participate and Colonel Blaskic would participate as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course or as a result of these meetings, were you able to learn something about his views, what was his role in terms of the process? What were his views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I feel that I got to know Colonel Blaskic very well. His position was the head of the Operational Zone Central Bosnia, and as such, was in a senior position, obviously, in terms of command over HVO soldiers. During the time I worked with him, I found him to be open and giving access to the international community. I certainly never had any problem having access myself to discuss matters. And my assessment was that I was dealing with a young but capable professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell whether he had respect for the international community and the European Union or did he exhibit a disrespect or a disregard for their views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He certainly had a respect for the European Community Monitoring Mission and I believe more widely a respect for the international community's views. It was important to the Croat community, but not only the Croat community, indeed any relatively isolated community, that they had the voice of the international community and that's what the ECMM could provide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he subscribe to an extremist political philosophy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not. I would characterise him as very much a professional soldier and distancing himself from political views. And I can give you an example of that in terms of -- at one stage, our task as monitors was to try and partially implement the Vance-Owen peace plan, and of course in order to do so, Bosnia had been organised in terms of -- or was going to be organised in terms of cantons, and Central Bosnia was one of those cantons and I needed to have the views obviously of senior people as to how they felt about this. And I discussed this with Colonel Blaskic and he told me that he dealt with reality on the ground and for political views I would need to speak to others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point in your dealings with him, did he exhibit any bias or animus towards Muslims or Muslim culture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Clearly, as the commander of HVO forces, he was engaged in combat with Armija forces, but in terms of a philosophy, an extremist philosophy, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get any feedback from officers in the BH army with respect to how they viewed then-Colonel Blaskic in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was important as monitors to get as much information as we could from different sources so that we could get a complete picture, and certainly discussing the merits and otherwise of opposing commanders was something which I took the opportunity to solicit their views, and I certainly discussed this with Mehmed Alagic, who was the operational group commander for 7 group based in Travnik at the time, who later became commander of 7th Corps, a respected military commander on the BH side, and he said that he respected Tihomir Blaskic as a former JNA soldier and nearly always when we spoke in terms of leadership in Central Bosnia, there was a distinction made between Colonel Blaskic and other political leaders, particularly Anto Valenta and Dario Kordic, who were very much the voice of some of the more extreme nationalist views that were being articulated in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these BH officers distinguish between these two --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- types, if you will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also actually spoke to General Hadzihasanovic, who at the time was the commander of 3rd Corps, and to his deputy, Dzemo Merdan, and again, I had the appreciation of a distinction between the leadership they were dealing with and a respect for Tihomir Blaskic, although I would add in the case of Hadzihasanovic, I think there was a certain sort of seniority aspect there, as I mentioned earlier, Colonel Blaskic was a relatively young colonel and Hadzihasanovic was, I think, a much more experienced JNA officer, and to a certain extent, I think that Hadzihasanovic played on that and wasn't going to give him any sort of equal status, although he was opposing him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to the characteristics of the HVO forces. Were there different pockets with respect to the territory that at least at one point in time was controlled by the HVO in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a difficult, an interesting landscape of military Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. activity. If I could actually come out of Central Bosnia to explain briefly in Herzegovina, where the Croat forces had two operational zones, operational zone north-west Herzegovina, which was commanded by General Siljeg, and the operational zone in Mostar, south-east Herzegovina. That area, they controlled all the territory, righted up to the front line, which ran from Prozor down through Jablanica and to the west side of the Neretva valley. And there, there was a coherent command and control and ability of leadership to move around that area. It was very different, once one crossed the front line which ran through Prozor, the Makljen ridge, and went down into the Vrbas valley and up into the Lasva Valley through Central Bosnia, where one had a series of pockets where you would have the largest pocket being the Croat community in Vitez and Busovaca. But within those pockets, other isolated communities, such as the Muslim community in Stari Vitez and Kruscica, so pockets within pockets and quite a complex picture. And as one moved further north-east, we had pockets around Vares and pockets around Zepce and Zavidovici, and pockets in Kiseljak area. So a fragmented picture of communities of various sizes, isolated, and then other communities within those isolated communities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On paper, did Colonel Blaskic have responsibility for the areas in these different pockets you've mentioned, Vares, Zepce, Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On paper, as the commander of the operational zone, he had command from Travnik through to -- south to Kiseljak, indeed, actually on paper to Sarajevo, further east. Yes, he commanded Vares pocket and also the Zepce, Zavidovici pocket. Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf actually came under the command of General -- or Colonel Siljeg, operational zone north-west Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We often hear the phrase in military parlance "command and control." What was the effect of the existence of these various pockets on HVO command and control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was a different picture to that I painted a moment ago in Herzegovina. In fact, for effective military operations, there are three Cs, as we are taught in the western armies. That's communications, command and control. And while all three of those important ingredients were in existence in Herzegovina, it was a different picture in Central Bosnia, where, through physical isolation, the task of a commander was considerably more difficult. Communications indeed were difficult, but I do know that there were communications between the operational zone headquarters, for instance, in Vitez and I saw myself a communication to Zepce. So there were communications. But as for the ability of the HVO for Colonel Blaskic to physically go to those pockets, no, that wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does that mean in terms of actual control? If you can't go, does that have an impact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does over time, I think, because what we observed were alternative -- or individual leaders emerging in those pockets. So, for instance, in Zepce and Zavidovici, we had Perica Jukic and Mr. Ivanovic, who were in command and making all sorts of local arrangements. Indeed, the pocket was difficult for us in the international community to get to ourselves, but I did successfully get there in early September 1993, not quite knowing what to expect in terms of the conditions of the community, and was surprised at how good they were, and discovered that the reason for that was that arrangements had been made with the Serbian community because there was a common front line between Serbian community and the Croatian pocket, and I think for all sorts of interests, ranging from trade, black market, self-preservation, arrangements had been made. So in that area, and Vares was very similar, indeed Kiseljak was the same. All three of those pockets had a common front line with Serb forces and to varying degrees, deals were done. In Vares, we had the Bobovac HVO and we had the mayor, I think was Ante Pejcinovic. I forget exactly his name. Zvonko Duzevic was a guy who we dealt with a lot there, a security officer, but I think his profile was actually higher than that. And the commander there was Kresimir Bozic initially. And on my visiting those people and observing what was going on there, I saw that they were in a position to control movements of people and trade, and so they were in a powerful position. And so yes, on paper, on the organogram, on our little things which we had pinned above our desks on who commanded what, Colonel Blaskic had command, on paper, of those people. But in terms of -- his ability to project that command was frustrated by the physical isolation. I have no doubt that there were times when orders would have been carried out, but if they chose not to because locally it didn't quite suit conditions, there was none of the means which a commander would need to be able to exert his authority, and so that, I think that difficulty would increase and did increase over time as well, as there was a certain confidence of the independent action in those pockets. The same happened in Kiseljak with the command there. We had the Ban Josip Jelacic command, and the commander there was Ivica Rajic, and we also dealt with a liaison officer called Lukic there. And they certainly had interesting relations with the Serbs, and again, when one looks in terms of availability of goods, of what was stocked in shops, you could see that there was trade and they were getting it from somewhere. And that was a different picture in the pocket in Kiseljak and Busovaca, which was one contiguous pocket, where certainly the situation was much harder, much more difficult and not the availability of the goods that I've just described, as we saw in those other pockets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Vitez and Busovaca was more isolated than these other pockets you've been talking about, which bordered on, at least some of which bordered on Serb-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go, since you're speaking of Kiseljak, we'll go to Kiseljak first and come back to some other areas. Did you obtain any other information while you were serving in the former Yugoslavia to give you a basis to comment more specifically on the Tihomir Blaskic-Ivica Rajic relationship and whether that was a command and control relationship, or at least at times merely a command relationship, without effective control by Tihomir Blaskic over Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was a communications link between the two, because of the physical isolation which I described, the command and control elements, which are important, were not easy to -- were not strong. In terms of links between Blaskic and Rajic, Rajic, on paper, came under his command. There was no doubt about that. The only time that I personally can directly link an incident or activity between the two was over an incident which took place in early October, mid-October, 1993, when a road was blown up. The road was the road between Visoko and Kiseljak. And it was quite a difficult thing to explain at the time, because this road was really only used by the international community, and so it seemed that the target of this action was not army of BiH but the international community. And of course we wanted this addressed. I suppose the international community, we could have filled it in ourselves, but I seem to remember at the time there being certainly a resistance from Rajic to us being able to do that, roadblocks. But specifically, because I was in Central Bosnia, I went to see Colonel Blaskic and demanded to know what was going on and what action was being taken, and I was told that it would -- it would be sorted. Well, several days later it still hadn't been sorted, so I went back to see Colonel Blaskic, and I was told that there were certain difficulties, that -- in getting Rajic to obey the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that -- is it normal for a professional soldier to be, if you will, sort of airing his dirty laundry to a member of the international community and complaining that he's having trouble controlling elements that on paper, at least, are to be -- should be subordinated to him, or was that somewhat unusual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was unusual. In fact, something which I would say would characterise Tihomir Blaskic was that there were times when I would like to have teased out a difference between himself and other commanders, and indeed between himself and some of the political leadership in the area. But he was actually resistant to that, and I very much interpreted that as a responsible professional soldier. You know, if you have undergone training, it is not the role of the soldier to criticise political masters, and I think history is probably littered with examples of people who tried that and got it wrong. So, it was unusual but he certainly did indicate on that occasion he was having difficulty, and he did actually on one other occasion tell me that he was having difficulty, and that was on a completely separate incident, and that was with regards to international community getting access to a village near Vitez, where the water supply to Vitez - it was Kruscica village - the water supply to Vitez was controlled there and Kruscica was a village -- was actually one of those pockets within a pocket. The Muslim community controlled it. And every now and again, the Muslim community would turn off the water and punish the larger Croat population of Vitez, and we of course would need to try and get this resolved. And access to that village was difficult, and on another occasion, I -- he did tell me that he was having difficulty with getting access because Mario Cerkez, the commander of the Vitez Brigade, was being difficult. But actually, I must qualify that slightly, because I'm not entirely sure it was Blaskic on that occasion. It may have been one of his staff that told me there was a difficulty. Overall, did Blaskic air his dirty linen in public, as you said earlier? No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you wouldn't have expect him to, given that he conducted himself in a professional manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. I would not have expected him to do that, and very rarely did he.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could just finish with Kiseljak before we move on to other topics. Did you learn in the course of your work that Ivica Rajic had a role in the black market in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, most definitely. There were -- we were very interested in this trade because of course it affected the balance of military capability or potentially could. If the Serbs were willing to do more than trade in food and we established -- I had a meeting with Filip Filipovic, who was one of the commanders in HVO operational zone. I think he might have been the deputy, but I could stand corrected on that. And he was telling me how much trade was going on and what certain things cost, and it did include cost of ammunition. So there was a lot of trade going on. And it was clear that that trade was controlled by the main leadership in the Kiseljak pocket. Rajic was certainly amongst those. I think also the mayor, whose name escapes me at the moment, may well have been involved. But certainly I saw evidence of the trade, and discussed evidence -- or discussed that trade with senior commanders in the operational zone headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that affect command and control relationships, if Ivica Rajic could obtain his own weapons on the black market, earn his own wealth through dealing in liquor, cigarettes, and the like, unlike persons in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the control and flow of those goods could make people and did make people extremely wealthy and powerful, and it could be that there were certainly times when the requirements of the operational zone, the military zone headquarters in Vitez, were in accordance with that general activity. But certainly, my belief is that instructions given that may have affected or in any way reduced the effectiveness of that control and command which Rajic had with partners in Kiseljak could be ignored.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether General Petkovic, the commander one level up from, for example, Colonel Blaskic, did he spend a lot of time in Kiseljak in 1993, from, say, the second half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't honestly say how much time he spent there, but certainly, yes, he was there. He was there for a number of reasons. The headquarters of the UN at the time was in Kiseljak, before it moved into -- later into Sarajevo, and there were many discussions held at Kiseljak. And I believe that he did have a facility - I don't know whether I call it a headquarters - but a facility in Kiseljak, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then if you have three levels of command - A, B, C - here it would be Petkovic, Blaskic, Rajic, but B is isolated in his own pocket and A and C are collocated, at least for significant periods of time in a different pocket, how would that further affect the control relationship between B and C, that is, Blaskic and Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would expect that it would give the opportunity for Petkovic to deal directly with Rajic in terms of which you presented it, A connected to C, without reference to Colonel Blaskic, B, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could come back now to the Vitez pocket. Did you have experiences on the ground which were instructive to you in terms of the degree of control that Colonel Blaskic had over HVO elements inside the Vitez pocket? You mentioned the Kruscica water experience, but are there other experiences such as at checkpoints where you gathered intelligence or other useful information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I would be probably at the risk of repeating myself, but when, for instance, I wished to get to Zepce, I certainly got the permission, both first of all of Blaskic and then of the Armija, because I was going through their territory, I saw indications of a communication between Zepce, in other words, that Zepce were expecting our arrival. But what was intriguing about this is, of course, the lack of information about the conditions in Zepce. Because on my return, of course, the one thing that Colonel Blaskic knows about is what is the situation like there. Now, we didn't trade intelligence, but certainly in terms of information that was not sensitive, about the humanitarian situation, then we would be happy to discuss that. So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is -- sorry to interrupt, but this is a pocket that he commanded on paper but he's asking you what's going on there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In terms of civilian population and, you know, what's the state of affairs there. Sorry. I was going to say that there were always rumours of atrocities, and often quite specific information about a number of people killed in a particular village and we would go and investigate those. And I do remember on my trip to Zepce, there being such a list. But when we get to the other end and when we discuss it, we find the situation is different and it's often, nearly always the case that we were unable to verify particular atrocities and that things had certainly happened, but had got exaggerated. Now, that's again an indication of being asked to find out about information. Well, if he had the ability to move to that area and to see for himself, then he would have had a more complete picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although in a military command, the commander is supposed to get reports from the field. Are you saying the mere ability to get reports and issue commands is not enough to have effective control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not enough to have effective command and control. And I'm not sure, I was never privileged to any signal intelligence how good the communications were. I simply can say I saw communications between those headquarters. There would be no land line, so this would have been a satellite fax or whatever communication. So, yeah, communications there, but even the communications would be difficult. So if I was the commander in that situation, I would not feel that I had complete command and control, even if I was able to communicate with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning again, if we could, to the Vitez pocket. Was there an attempt to evacuate wounded from the Travnik hospital at some point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was personally involved in several attempts to evacuate hospitals. Travnik is one example, Nova Bila another, and later in Mostar. In the case of Travnik, which you ask, when I got into Central Bosnia in late May/early June 1993, we were still in a position where we were hoping to avoid conflict between the Croat and Armija forces. We had a joint command which the international community brokered and the ECMM was very much involved with, which on paper anyway, this joint command existed in Travnik, and I was involved in -- actually physically based in Travnik myself and moved my headquarters there, as part of a confidence-building statement, which proved to be somewhat futile because only a matter of days after locating there, the conflict between the two, the Croats and Muslims, broke out in earnest and the HVO were -- withdrew, defeated, driven out of Travnik. That was complicated in itself, and if necessary, I could explain the differences I hint at there. But the result was casualties, and the Travnik hospital we visited because not just if I'm brutally honest, the humanitarian situation, but it was an indication of how fierce fighting was, the number of casualties is a clear indicator. And so I went to try and see what the situation was like, and I saw something there which I saw again in other areas, which -- very difficult circumstances, very overcrowded, people with pretty horrific wounds, people stacked in corridors on trolleys, something you don't want to see. I decided it would be a good idea to try and evacuate this hospital. It was actually a hospital that had -- it had Croats, women, children, Muslims. So I could see an opportunity, rather callously, perhaps, to try and negotiate something. ICRC were particularly nervous about this, as were UNPROFOR. Their mandates were being stretched. There was fighting. Where were they going to be taken to, the casualties, the ICRC would never move people if they were going to go into an area that was still in fighting, and in the case of the Croats, the plan was that we would take the Croat casualties to Nova Bila and that we would take the Muslim casualties to Travnik. UNPROFOR's mandate was quite restricted. They were very, very concerned at the time about what they called mission creep, which was being asked to do things beyond the mandate. So it was left to organisations such as ourselves which had a degree of flexibility, had a degree of independence and a most astonishingly wide open memoranda of understanding which allowed us to do all sorts of things, to organise something. So I got the agreement of military commanders on the Armija side. I believe that it was Alagic and I think Merdan, rather than Hadzihasanovic, and on the Croat side, it was Nakic and Blaskic, Franjo Nakic and Blaskic. And the agreement was we could do this, but -- so I went to the UN. The UN said they would provide a military presence on the route. I got into Travnik. I explained to the doctors what we were going to do. They organised transport and ambulances. I think one ambulance, the rest cars and stuff. And I ensured that while they chose the worst -- that it must include, I stated, women and children, elements of Croats -- because it was a convoy which needed to contain -- I know this sounds terribly callous, but it needed to contain both communities in order to be successful. So once loaded, we left Travnik, travelling south down the Lasva Valley towards our first destination, which was to be Nova Bila. And we got to a point known as Dolac, the Dolac checkpoint. The Dolac checkpoint was an important checkpoint, and it was just behind what was a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relatively, at that stage, fluid front line, and it was controlled by the HVO. It was important because it was at a junction of a road which went from that main Vitez-Travnik road north across a sort of back route to Zenica, through villages like Guca Gora, Brajkovici, Pranjkovici, Maline. If you have a map I could show you. But it's an important checkpoint, because who controlled that, controlled access to Zenica. And at that checkpoint, as I drove leading this convoy, there was a very excited reception from HVO soldiers who were well armed, right in the middle of the road, a guy with a rocket-propelled grenade pointing directly at my vehicle, and a physical checkpoint, a little box off to the right-hand side. There were soldiers in there, soldiers taking up firing positions and obviously preventing my continued safe passage. So at that point I got out and went through what was almost a daily activity in Bosnia, negotiating your way through checkpoints. And this was different because we could hear firing. I say it was behind a relatively fluid front line. And these guys see us coming out of the territory controlled by the Armija and they were very excited. So I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened? We have about 15 more minutes to finish your testimony, so if we could focus in on what happened at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. At the checkpoint, I was stopped, and they -- I said that I had permission to do this, I had permission of the senior Croat commanders, and that I had the permission of Colonel Blaskic. And the response was: "We do not report or take orders from Colonel Blaskic." What happened then is the leader of this group said he was going to ask his commander. I didn't ask who his commander was, but he was going to ask his commander what to do. So he departed. I tried in that period to negotiate with the others to get through. They wouldn't let me through. He returned after an hour, hour and a half, on an extremely hot day. Conditions in the vehicles were appalling, and he got out and he said: "Okay. We will let the Croats through. I want you to separate the Croats from the others." I said that was not possible. Clearly, separation would have been impossible and wrong. So I said I couldn't do that, but I appealed to him on humanitarian grounds. At that point, he cocked his weapon, aimed it directly at me, and in a gesture of okay, "we've gone as far as we can, I'm going to get in the car, turn the convoy around, and I'm going to go back," and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you comfortable representing to the Court this is an instance where Colonel Blaskic's orders that this humanitarian convoy be allowed to passed, his orders were not followed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His orders were not followed and I was told by that checkpoint that they did not take orders from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far was this from the Hotel Vitez, Colonel Blaskic's command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In terms of how long it would take to get there, I guess 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Franjo Nakic. Was he the deputy? Was he Colonel Blaskic's deputy or another high-ranking officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was certainly a high-ranking officer within the operational zone. I forget whether he was deputy or chief of staff. It was either Filip Filipovic who was deputy or Franjo Nakic who was deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- sorry. Had Nakic been a -- did he have professional military training; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nakic, no. He was a nice guy in military uniform but I believe he had actually run a factory, a clothing factory, I think. Filipovic was JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Vitez area, were there units that you recognised as special units on the part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Vitez-Busovaca pocket, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is a special unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was a unit to us that had a coherence and an identity which was somewhat different to the HVO soldier one would come across at checkpoints. And by coherence, I mean all wearing the same uniform, well equipped, often equipped with the same weaponry. In the case of the Vitez-Busovaca pocket, there were -- there was one group in particular that were based off the main road. In Busovaca, in something which was known to us as the Swiss chalet. It was a restaurant or hotel or something like that. And there was a unit there which we knew as the Jokers, who were one such special unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you obtain any information during your tour of duty that would give you any insights into the command and control over this unit, the Jokers unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Jokers unit were, we believed, a unit who reported to Dario Kordic. I did meet the leader of the Jokers, Furundija [phoen], Anton. I forget exactly his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's it, Furundzija. But in fact, my information about these Jokers were really got from a number of sources, and those sources would be what UNPROFOR's view were of them, quite critically and quite importantly what the local staff who worked with us, interpreters, drivers, thought, and also crucially what information we got when we spoke to the Armija BiH officers. And from that triangulation of information, it was my understanding that those special units reported to Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your view an outlier view or was your view on this very important subject commonly held among the ECMM monitors and professional staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would describe it as conventional wisdom that those were reporting to Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you gain insights during your work as to the relationship between Tihomir Blaskic and Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. These were the two main Croat individuals who we dealt with. Kordic could be characterised as primarily dealing with political issues, although he somewhat clouded that by sometimes presenting himself indeed as a colonel and being seen in uniform. But in the case of Blaskic, he was the professional soldier and distanced himself from the political affairs. I think I gave an example earlier on of the Vance-Owen Plan, when he said I should speak to those in charge of political activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you gain any information from any sources with respect to whether there were disagreements between these two men, that is, whether Colonel Blaskic necessarily shared political views held by Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that Colonel Blaskic was always very sort of discreet, as I say, and to me that was a mark of his professionalism. But to us, there was a gap, and we wanted to find out about this gap, and so we would take the chance while we were waiting to see the more senior people, such as Anto Valenta and the colonel himself, to talk to the other staff. Darko Gelic, in particular, the liaison officer at the headquarters spoke good English, was perhaps less discreet and I believe without meaning to gave us information. And he would -- he certainly gave me the absolute impression that they considered the presence, the physical presence of Anto Valenta in that headquarters as something that was uncomfortable, and they had quite a sort of disparaging view of Valenta in that he would sometimes be indicated to be off the wall. I do remember Darko Gelic laughing and smiling when I asked about some of the views of Anto Valenta. He tapped his head. So from the staff one got the feeling that there was a tolerance, but an awkwardness between the physical proximity of the political voice in terms of Valenta in the headquarters and Blaskic. And there were times when I needed to do things which I needed Blaskic's permission, for instance, to get into Stari Vitez. And on one occasion when I wanted to do that, it was to actually take a Muslim doctor that was much needed in Stari Vitez, and I went to Blaskic to say: "Look, I'm taking a doctor through and I don't want there to be any incidents. And I need a clear run." And he said that he would need to discuss, and I would need to come back before I could do that. In fact, I did go back the next day, the day after, and did get access, but he had indicated to me that he was referring to someone, because this seemed sensitive. And I assumed, though I did not ask him, that that was the political leadership, either Kordic or Valenta. I think probably you asked about the relationship between Kordic and Blaskic. I think that it was probably the communication with Blaskic rather than Valenta, because Valenta was something of a figure of fun in that headquarters, although one should take seriously in other ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's an issue in this case whether the use of certain military tactics are sufficiently unique to constitute a signature or a pattern from which certain inferences can be drawn, and namely the pattern is the beginning of an attack, an artillery attack followed by an infantry offensive. Is that a distinctive pattern, or a signature type of pattern of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a straightforward military technique. I mean, if one is engaged in combat, you use whatever resources you have in your command to bring to bear firepower, and a way to firepower. And so I -- I mean, here, if you're asking if -- one moment. Can I just read? Artillery attack followed by infantry offensive is standard, would be taught in any military academy that you bring whatever firepower you have and artillery is a weapon that is used, is an area weapon, that is, it's not a precise weapon. It is used to cause confusion and one would soften up a target prior to infantry attack. It's a standard military practice. It would not mean that because of seeing that combination you could say: "Ah, this is the obvious work of a particular commander." It's what every second lieutenant at Sandhurst would be taught on day five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other question about a military term and then I'll wrap up. Are you familiar with the term "mop-up"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mop-up, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's after intense activity, one can go from -- there's levels of intensity of activity, and so after maybe an attack, there would be pockets that one could in a military have left because they were particularly difficult, so one bypasses. And then having won the main objective, you would go back and sort out, either surrender or destroy the enemy, and that action after the main event, when the intensity is reduced to a low intensity activity, that mopping up is the complete control that you wish to have over your territory and the clearing of enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a standard military term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any connotation in the use of that term that would suggest harm to civilians or ethnic cleansing or something of the like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, although seeing it on the screen and hearing it, as you say, of course it's what I would call in England an insensitive, politically incorrect thing, but it is standard military terminology. Anyone in the military would understand this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now just in closing I would like you to go back to the 1990s. Do you remember when you were first interviewed by the Prosecutor's office or their representatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The first time I ever came across ICTY was actually when I was still head of the regional centre in Bosnia when there was a visit, but in terms of interviewing me for my experiences, the first formal one was in the United Kingdom, and it would have been somewhere in 1996, 1997, when investigators came to England and for a couple of days interviewed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you what case they were preparing for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told me that they were dealing with Croat issues. They told me that they wanted to discuss in broad terms my understanding and experiences and recollections. But at that stage, I -- I mean, one can guess, if we're talking about Central Bosnia and we're talking about Croats, that we're talking about the key people. But no, not specifically that I was giving evidence on one case or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're aware that Colonel Blaskic's trial began in 1997, or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, thereabouts. I know that Colonel Blaskic volunteered, as I understand it, and got on a plane and was one of the first to come here. The exact date I simply cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of the investigators who interviewed you in the 1996, 1997 time frame, are they still around? Are they still working for the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to pose an objection at this point. I don't see the relevance of this for any purpose, but certainly not on appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The relevance, Your Honours, is this witness told the Prosecutor's office in '96, in substance what he's told Your Honours today. The Prosecutor's office suppressed that information from the Blaskic Defence. They used it in the Kordic trial, continued to suppress it, and to this day they will not produce the statement that they took from this man in 1996. They won't give him a copy and they won't produce it to us, and that needs to be part of the record here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If I may respond to this. That's completely inaccurate. This witness was contacted and asked whether he wanted his statement. We had dealt with this matter, and the fact that the claim is that we wouldn't give a copy to this witness is, as I understand it, incorrect. I can certainly clarify that and get back to you; if I am incorrect I'll inform you. My understanding is this witness was contacted. If Mr. Hayman would like to make some legal arguments on issues related to Rule 68, the material is on the record and he's certainly able to do so. I don't know whether he should be doing it through a witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness, Your Honour. Let's ask him. Did he give a statement? Did he sign a statement, ask for a copy? Has he consistently been denied a copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. This question you can put.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was asked to make a signed statement. I did make a signed statement. It was printed off in front of me. I asked for a copy. I was not given a copy. I did see that copy again in preparation for the Kordic trial, when I was shown it by Mr. Geoffrey Nice, when he interviewed me in London, and he asked me if there was anything in that statement that I substantially disagreed with, and there was nothing. I said no. That statement is true. But I certainly asked for a copy and I was not given a copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over how many days were you interviewed by the Prosecutor's office in the 1996, 1997 time period? You've testified today for a little less than one hour. How long was your interview with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was certainly two days, possibly three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you cover in that interview in substance what you've discussed here today, but in much more detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes our direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. May I now turn to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, out of abundant caution, may we go to private session for a moment on a procedural matter, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now, since we are in open session, there is another matter I would like to address. The Bench met over the break and decided that, on the basis of what we learnt during the examination-in-chief, the Prosecution be requested to produce the document -- the statement of the witness Watkins, that would be under Rule 98 of the Rules. I would request that it be produced at the end of the cross-examination, before re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'd be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Scott, you can proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President Cross-examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I -- good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand your prior testimony correctly, you consider -- you considered at the time and would still consider that Dario Kordic was, on the HVO side, the top political leader in Central Bosnia who had a great deal of influence on the course of events in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, and Anto Valenta was the other senior member of the political community there, also, I understand, a vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So, on paper, similar status, but Kordic was, in my mind, the key person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your dealings with Mr. Kordic, sir, as you described to the Chamber earlier, would you describe Mr. Kordic, if you will, as a big-picture thinker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I met Mr. Kordic, I would speak about a range of activity, some military, some political. He called himself a colonel, but it was clear that he was uncomfortable with detail that -- of discussions on military terms and wanted to talk more about some big ideas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that respect, sir, would it be fair to say that in the course of any meetings or discussions you had with Mr. Kordic, he never displayed to you a detailed knowledge of military matters or military planning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he felt uncomfortable certainly in discussions with me. I had a military training, and I was able on a number of occasions, one in particular about a shelling of Zenica, to give him detail to demonstrate my own knowledge of military activity, and I think he felt a little bit uncomfortable. He presented himself as a colonel, but he wasn't a military-trained individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you, as a trained, professional military officer, wanted to engage in discussion about military matters, who would you go to? Colonel Blaskic or Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would you also agree, sir, that Mr. Kordic had a great deal of influence and essentially, if you will, in fact, control over Mr. or Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relationship between the two of them was, of course, interesting. Control over him, I do believe that ultimately, yes, there was, as the senior political person there, he would be able to influence, instruct, Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, when you were in the field at the time, on the 28th of August, 1993, in one of your reports, your daily summary, you said that: "Dario Kordic is the key HDZ political figure in Central Bosnia and has long been suspected of controlling the HVO. It is assessed that his influence over Blaskic is significant, if not total."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you'll read it directly from that report, that roughly chimes, but I haven't seen it to confirm. But yes, I would stand by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the fact that Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic held a weekly press briefing together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't know it was weekly. They certainly had press briefings. But I actually never in my time there saw them together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, sir, that Kordic and Blaskic, during this time worked very closely together and some might even say they were two sides of the same coin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can understand why you would say that, two sides of the same coin, I mean. Certainly they were the key leaders of the Croat community. There was no doubt. But I think it would be a flawed thesis to see them as motivated in the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you gave some indication that there was a widely shared views in the international community on the ground at the time that the two of them are about concerning Mr. or Colonel Blaskic and about his professionalism, but, sir, wasn't it also the view of many in that community that, in fact, as one British reported -- reported in one British battalion daily report, they were two bodies, one brain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can imagine that the author of that sentence was probably quite pleased with himself, because it has a certain sort of -- it explains it succinctly as he saw it, and I guess also there's a slightly condescending tone in there as well. It's not the way that I would describe it. I think it's a little bit superficial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You arrived in Central Bosnia, or the Lasva Valley, in particular, in about May, at the end of May or early June 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was in Central Bosnia in February, because Gornji Vakuf was my base, and that was Central Bosnia. In terms of me becoming head of regional centre and working in the Vitez-Busovaca-Lasva Valley area, you're correct; it was end of May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Chamber should understand that your observations and assessments about what was happening in the Lasva Valley are primarily focussed on the time from the beginning of June 1993 until approximately mid-October, when you went to Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Late May/early June. But that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony in the Kordic case, and today, about certain enclaves developing, that testimony focussed primarily on Zepce and Vares, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think I mentioned Sarajevo, and also Kiseljak. But yeah, I guess the emphasis and weight probably was I spoke more about Zepce, Zavidovici, and Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you responded to a question from counsel that whether in fact the Busovaca-Vitez enclave was somehow even more cut off, you didn't mean more cut off from the other parts of the Bosnian Croat community, did you? Because weren't Vares and Zepce in fact substantially more cut off in that respect than Busovaca and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a difference in scale, but no, actually, there was easier movement for the Croat community from the pockets of Vares, Zepce, and Kiseljak than there was from the pocket of Vitez and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I understand your view on that, it's because there was a fair amount of deal-making with the Serb side, which allowed Bosnian Croats to travel through otherwise Serb-controlled areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. And a good example of that would be movements of population that came into Herzegovina through the Stolac checkpoint down near Mostar, and to the north, at Celebici, which is up near -- north of Tomislavgrad, north-west of Tomislavgrad. So there was movement through the Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, sir, this was not -- these sorts of deals with the Serbs if you will were not limited to people like Mr. Rajic or Vares or Zepce but were conducted at the highest levels of the Bosnian Croat leadership, correct, including for instance at the level of Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand so. But I think it's important to point out that there was no front line between the Vitez-Busovaca pocket and the Croat -- and the Serb community. So in order for someone to move from the Vitez-Busovaca pocket, they would have to have gone through Armija BiH held territory and that is substantially different from the situation in Zepce, Vares, and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir would you agree with me as a professional soldier or at least formerly so that a criminal order can be given just as much on a telephone as it can in a face-to-face conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess that would be right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me, would you not, that if a senior commander were to order his subordinates on the telephone to use captured prisoners to dig fortifications or dig trenches, I think was commonly how it's described, in dangerous combat conditions, that would be an illegal order, whether or not it was stated on the telephone or face to face; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. If you could prove that it had actually been spoken on the telephone or spoken face to face. But yeah, that would be an illegal order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And an order to conceal a crime, a crime that had already been committed, but an order to conceal a crime that was accomplished by telephone would equally be just as bad as one communicated in person; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that in connection with a senior commander, he might receive -- he or she might receive information by fax or by telephone or whatever means sufficiently such that it would put him on notice, if you will, on duty to inquire about the existence or possible happening of crimes in areas under his responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly there could be communications, as you've described, and I don't disagree with what you said there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concerning Kiseljak, it's correct, is it not, sir, that while it may or may not, but for arguments's sake, while it may have been cut off physically for a time from the Vitez-Busovaca area, there were still a number of communications available, including what was called packet communications, faxes, telephones, and the like; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say there was no argument that it was physically cut off. It was physically cut off. In terms of communication, I'm not sure about the land line, because certainly I do not remember us being able to make calls ourselves. And we're back, I think, to this issue which I was asked about earlier of communications, sure. Does that mean that the communications can then be translated into command and control at the other end? That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if the witness could please be provided a binder of exhibits to be used with the witness. It should have been -- I'm sorry. If the usher could assist me. And I believe, Mr. President, a set of exhibits were prepared and distributed to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, what kind of documents are in the binders?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: These are all previously admitted documents, Mr. President, and it's just simply, rather than have the usher hand him one document at a time, this is simply to facilitate. Our time is very limited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention, please, and the courtroom's attention, to tab 19 of the binders, or otherwise Exhibit PA15. You said in direct examination, sir, that Blaskic respected the international community and gave access to them. Were you aware, sir, that on the 18th of April, 1993, Colonel Blaskic issued an order to block UN peacekeeping forces from entering certain areas, and in fact, authorised HVO forces to fire on UN vehicles and forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of this. I'm not entirely surprised. Certainly, there were times when access for all international communities was difficult. Sometimes it would be a selected international community organisation. But by and large, and over a period of time, my assessment is that I was, through direct contact, with Blaskic able to gain access to the most difficult places which were in his control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you seen this order before? Have you specifically seen this order before where Colonel Blaskic ordered HVO forces to block UN access to certain areas, in mid-April, while the events in the Lasva Valley were occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen this order yesterday, when I spoke with the Defence counsel, but I was not aware of it before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you ask you, please, to direct your attention to tab 29 of that same binder, Exhibit PA51. This is an order by Colonel Blaskic to the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak on the 22nd of April, 1993, where he instructs that HVO unit to implement tasks couched as response to provocations and tells them, orders them: Always justify my orders as response to provocations from the other side. Have you seen that order before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've not seen this order. Can I just take a moment to read it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you ask you to turn to tab 32, Exhibit PA52. It's another order by Colonel Blaskic to, again, the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak. This supposedly cut off Kiseljak. In which Colonel Blaskic says: "Do not allow the representatives of ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross, to visit facilities other than official detentions, and do not admit that there are any other detainees anywhere else." Have you seen that order before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this one. I saw this one yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please direct your attention to tab 33, the next document, Exhibit PA56. Again, an order to -- by Colonel Blaskic to the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak, the 22nd of May, 1993. I won't read it verbatim. Everyone has it in front of them. But basically, saying: In connection with a detainee who had been killed while digging trenches, be careful about how that information is reported, because if UNPROFOR, the ECMM, and others obtain this information, they will blame the HVO for improper treatment. Were you ever aware that Colonel Blaskic issued orders to block international community members from visiting detention facilities and from reporting the fact that there had been mistreatment of prisoners held by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm seeing the same document as you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's tab -- I've just been told -- my apologies to the witness and the Chamber. I've just been told it's tab 35.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw this document yesterday as well for the first time. Sorry. You'll have to ask your question again or I'll have to read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is simply this, after look at those four documents: Isn't it fair, sir, that at the time you were on the ground in Central Bosnia, that you had, as active as I'm sure you were on the ground, you nonetheless had the view of an outsider looking in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course I was not a member of any of the ethnic groups there, but I was a very informed outsider looking in. I was there, I believe, probably for longer than any other international monitor, although there may be one or two others. I could stand corrected on that. But a long time and so it was a very informed position. But sure, an outsider.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were a very informed person who had never seen any of these four orders before; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hadn't seen these communications, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact you never sat in on any internal HVO military planning sessions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never sat on any meetings where Dario Kordic and Colonel Blaskic discussed military matters and planned military strategy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw those --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Assumes a fact not in evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the evidence is all over the record. That's what this case is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where? Let's have an example. Let's have evidence of a meetings where internal military strategy was planned by Colonel Blaskic and Dario Kordic. If counsel is so sure of it, let's see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, it goes directly to the issue about meetings that have been all over the face of these pleadings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One example. Give us one example, Your Honours. That's what I ask for. Otherwise it's blunderbuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, can you make a precise reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not going to take the limited time I have to do that, and I guess Mr. Farrell, when he addresses the Chamber next week, there will be many references in the record to that. It goes to the witness's knowledge, in any event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point of the question is, sir, you were not privy, if you will, to internal HVO decision-making; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was, of course, at various meetings where we discussed with HVO about how they would respond or react, and indeed negotiations, but I was never on any occasion privy to sit at the back of my meeting between Blaskic and his HVO commanders discussing particular operational orders, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Blaskic was not particularly involved in political matters, sir, but I'd like to direct your attention and ask the usher's assistance to put on the ELMO Exhibit 456/109. Mr. President, this is a document not in the binder, one the relevance of which developed during the course of direct examination, but it has been previously admitted. I can give the Chamber -- the usher my copy, if you wish. Trial Exhibit -- admitted trial Exhibit 456/109. Sir, this is a record of the meeting of the local HVO-HDZ leadership in the Busovaca-Vitez area on the 22nd of September, 1992. The Chamber can and you can scan the participants and the content of the document, which I submit to you, sir, I put to you, is highly political. And if you look at the members of the working presidency, the working presidency is Dario Kordic, Anto Valenta, Tihomir Blaskic, and Ignac Kostroman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 22nd of September, 1992, no. I was in the British armed forces in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher's assistance, please, to put on the ELMO again admitted trial Exhibit 456/112. You mentioned, Colonel Blaskic's desire not to become involved in discussions of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of a senior ECMM representative or official named Thebault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jean-Pierre Thebault was the head of the regional centre in Zenica when I was the head of coordination centre in Travnik. We worked closely Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. together on Vance-Owen Plan. Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you would just scan that document briefly, please, in the interests of time. Is that not in fact a letter from Colonel Blaskic talking about the implementation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me to be discussing the -- or directed to the commander of 3rd Corps, another military commander, about emerging consequences. And as the senior military commander in Central Bosnia, it seems that he's using Jean-Pierre Thebault as a route to that other command. I see nothing particularly interesting about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance. Yes, Judge Schomburg. I apologise. If the usher could assist us to move the document down, and you could see the dates of that document and the addressee. The 26th of May, 1993, to the ECMM, Mr. Thebault.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you had not seen that document before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said at one point that the isolation of certain areas in enclaves or being cut off would have an effect over time on the way that activities were conducted in that so-called enclave. The Kiseljak area was not in fact cut off until sometime during the second half of April 1993, after the HVO attacks in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure the exact time that that -- those pockets were separated. I would have to see a document to see some sort of reference to the date. I really don't know. It's certainly, by the time I got into the Lasva Valley, was a distinct Vitez-Busovaca pocket and separate Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you had said -- the point of your testimony, what you had stayed, sir, was this would have -- as time went by, as the isolation continued over time, there might be effects on the way business, if you will, was conducted. But in fact as of the middle of April 1993, there had been no enclave. Kiseljak had immediate communication approximately 42 kilometres away from Vitez and Busovaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm uncomfortable about directly answering that without knowing or seeing reference to when that pocket was cut, because that would guide my answer. I don't know whether that's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about the ability to enforce command and exercise discipline. Did you ever know that in the course of your work in Bosnia of HVO officers being dismissed or discharged as a disciplinary matter for war crimes or misconduct that had occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For misconduct, yes. Actually, to be absolutely -- I'm not sure that they were finally dismissed, but we had a couple of incidents which involved transfers of individuals from Vitez to Travnik, and on one occasion it all went rather horribly wrong and my monitors were -- they were opened fire upon. Luckily, no casualties, but as a result of that, I made a direct and strong complaint to Blaskic and actually received a written reply explaining the situation, explaining that military action would be taken. But I can't say that I followed it right through to see what happened to those individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any instance, sir, can you tell these Judges of any instance in which Colonel Blaskic, to your knowledge, exercised military discipline over an HVO member for misconduct or commission of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the intention to do so, not the final outcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean his stated-to-you intention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stated intention to me. I don't know whether it helps at all, but also during the period that I was in Vitez, there was a change of military commander or actually leadership of the military police, from Ljubicic to another guy, Marinko, I think his name was, and I was interested in that. I'm not sure why that happened, but there were rumours that there had been disagreements and there was an order from on high that that leadership should change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Going to specifically Colonel Blaskic's control or dealings with this Ivica Rajic in Kiseljak. If I understand your prior testimony in the Kordic case and your testimony today - and correct me, sir, if I'm wrong - the only specific incident, the only specific item that you based that on, is an episode where Colonel Blaskic had ordered a road to be repaired and it wasn't repaired as quickly as one might have liked. Is that the only thing we're talking about here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Actually, there's one other, and that is, of course, -- not of course, but it is the involvement of Ivica Rajic in the Stupni Do massacre, which happened just after my move from Central Bosnia down to Mostar. And it's -- after ECMM inquiries, it became clear that Ivica Rajic had been involved in that at Vares [phoen], and I do not believe that there was any suggestion or connection that that action had resulted from a direct command from Blaskic. There was certainly no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor was there any indication, was there, that Colonel Blaskic took any effect or action to discipline or remove Mr. Rajic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that action, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Rajic in fact, contrary to what was told to the international community at the time, assumed another name and continued in the same chain of command, under Colonel Blaskic, after the international community had been told that he had been removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did know that he changed his name, and I think it was to something like Viktor Andric or something like that. But with regards to the ability of the commander, we keep coming back to this. He may send signals, but there was no way in which, if a signal had been sent about his dismissal, that Blaskic would actually be able to enforce that himself, but he could of course refer to Petkovic who might have physical proximity and been able to enable that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did he try, did he make an effort to remove Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I personally know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it influence your view, sir, over the existence of command and control between Colonel Blaskic and Kiseljak if there was a substantial record of communications, multiple communications each day, between Colonel Blaskic himself or his headquarters and the HVO units in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would prove to me that there were communications. It would not prove to me that there was command and control, unless I see some substance within those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it affect your view, sir, if not only were there communications, but there were orders going to Kiseljak, if you will, and responses and reports coming back from Kiseljak, indicating that Colonel Blaskic's orders were being carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would -- there would be no credibility to that communication if you saw the issuing of a command and a direct response to that than if you saw an issuing of a command and no response. Of course, that commander would not be able to know whether that order had actually taken place. He would only know that he had a response to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance to put before the witness the so-called war diary, which I believe is Defence Exhibit 14 on appeal and was Exhibit -- I'm sorry. That's from the Kordic case, but it's Exhibit -- I think Defence Exhibit 14 on appeal. If I could -- if that could please be put before the witnesses, and the Judges may wish to refer to that if they have it available to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, if I can please direct your attention and the Chamber's attention to page 73 of the English version, to the entry for the 16th of April, at 1000 hours, on page 73. And what I'm going to try to do, sir, is move, because my time is very limited, to a couple of entries, quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I inquire, Your Honours: Do you have page 73? No. My apologies. Perhaps it can be placed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Witness, does it say, at 1000 hours on the 16th of April: "At 1000 hours, Colonel T Blaskic talked with the commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, gave instructions about the situation and how to behave"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
