utterances.text: Yes, it says that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please go to page 95, 16th of April, at 1843 hours. "Communication to M Miletic for the Kiseljak Brigade. Hold those two Muslims until further notice." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can ask you, please, to go to page 107, 17th of April, at 0940 in the morning. "Provisional combat order of the 17th of April at 0910. The commander of the Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade, Kiseljak, for tying down the part of the Muslim forces attacking the HVO."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can next ask -- I just have two more. Page 137. Page 137, the 19th of April, at 0845. "Order of the 19th of April, 1993, at 0835, for Ban Jelacic, capturing Gomionica, deadline today."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, on page 148, the 20th of April, at 1302. Colonel TB speaking with Mijo Bozic, the head, the commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade. "This hill must be held. What are your positions up there? Are they in every bunker by the radar? What is the situation with Visnjica? What about Gomionica? Croats are being massacred in Zenica. It will be your turn if that is being asked is not done. The police will be used for cleansing and the military for breaking through. Keep pushing. If you fail to accomplish this, I am finished and then so are you. Stipo has no business promising. Things must be done as ordered, as you too take over," and it becomes illegible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that. Can I just check the date? You refer to a date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. If you're going to check, you'll have to leaf back, because these entries go on for some way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see what you're asking me to look at. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I've just picked five examples, but have you seen any of those communications at the very time in question, between Colonel Blaskic and his headquarters and the command of the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've never seen those before, and I wasn't in the Lasva Valley in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher's assistance to -- and again, not in the binders, but for the ELMO, please - Exhibit 456 -- trial exhibit admitted, Mr. President, 456/32. Sir, this is a -- sorry. I'll wait for you. This is a report down some pages into the document, you'll see by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, on the 7th of May, 1993, to the supreme commander of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the head of the defence department, and the chief of the main headquarters, which I believe at that time, you'll agree, sir, was Mr. Petkovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The head of the defence department at that time I believe was Stojic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to turn down - and unfortunately, the pages aren't numbered - but if you will go down about to the tenth page in that stack, please. If I can direct your attention to the paragraph under the paragraph numbered 6. Do you see the -- I think that's -- yeah. Previous page, but ... I'm looking at page -- that's not -- the page on the ELMO is not the page I'm looking at. Sir, do you see Colonel Blaskic at this very time in question, on the 7th of May, reporting to his top superiors, the very head of the HVO military in Mostar. Below paragraphs numbered 6, "all units are carrying out their tasks, except for the battalion in Fojnica, which is engaged in personnel reshuffling and taking a neutral position vis-a-vis the Muslims so the Muslim forces are attacking on Busovaca unimpeded from the area of Fojnica." And also on the next page, "Conclusion number 1: Command and control function properly and all missions proceed in a planned fashion according to orders, with detailed knowledge of the situation, full coordination and control."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that. Can I make a comment on the previous? Because it seems to be --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my time is extremely limited. Had you ever seen this document before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you, and I begin to wrap up, Mr. President, Exhibit from the Blaskic Prosecution Exhibit BP380, which again is an admitted exhibit. Now, sir, this is a translation of an interview that Colonel Blaskic gave on October -- in October of 1993. If you can -- if the usher can move that down. Well, no, it's fine. It's fine. At the top, the reporter is asking questions specifically about Kresevo, Kiseljak, and part of Fojnica municipality, but are not connected with the forces in Vitez and Busovaca. How are they holding up? Blaskic goes on, and he says: "They are carrying out, in a coordinated and organised manner, all commands connected with the defence of the people and Croatian territories. This physical separation is not an essential or decisive factor, because we figured in our planning that the temporary physical separation of these areas could occur." Going to the last sentence: "All operative groups are under my command, and the chain of leadership and command functions absolutely, without interruption." Have you seen Blaskic's assessment of his command and control, first the one on the 7th of May, the document I showed you a moment ago, and again in October of 1993, the same year? Have you seen either of those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've seen this document before. Can I just confirm it is a press document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lovrenovic, was he in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's an interview of General Blaskic, sir, Colonel Blaskic, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm not sure whether I'm allowed to ask questions. I'm just interested whether Lovrenovic actually met Blaskic, whether he was a journalist working --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can look at the fuller version of the B/C/S version is attached, if it will assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, since counsel has gone over his time, I assume I'll have more time on redirect as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Certainly we'll take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My point was simply whether this was a journalist who spoke to Blaskic or not, directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it appears to be a journalist asking questions, sir, and I agree: I don't want to pretend that I know with hundred per cent certainty, but it appears to be a published interview with a reporter asking questions and Colonel Blaskic giving answers and you have in front of you the full text, with a picture of Colonel Blaskic in the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And as a press report, one would be interested in who the audience of that press was and one would not expect Blaskic to be saying anything other than really I can see there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you wouldn't expect him to also be admitting to you the commission of crimes, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't expect him to admit them to me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am going to conclude. One piece of paper, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, did you know a person named Alastair Duncan, who was the commander of British Battalion during part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He commanded the Prince of Wales' Own, the second British battalion to deploy to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the field in that capacity during the period including June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact dates, but certainly I was part of his introduction, so I was already up there. It could have been late June, but certainly June, July, he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally involved with Alastair Duncan in the negotiations to allow the free passage of a convoy, of a convoy or convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Convoy of Joy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that Commander Duncan was fully aware of the same incident which you've testified about today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness didn't have any testimony about the Convoy of Joy. I don't know what the counsel is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me assist. The convoy of June 11th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the convoy you were talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't mentioned it today, but I did mention it in the Kordic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The convoy today was from the hospital in Travnik carrying wounded. The Convoy of Joy was some 400 or 500 trucks carrying humanitarian supplies, so counsel is talking about a different issue not discussed in my examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just have your confirmation, sir: Commander Duncan was involved in that particular matter, that June 11th convoy matter, with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's beyond the scope of the examination. If the Court wants to let counsel run with this, I don't care, but I want to go into it and have time to do it on redirect. I think it's helpful information but I held myself to the hour limit and didn't go into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I think Mr. Hayman is correct in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Let me just consult with Mr. Farrell, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I appreciate the Court's indulgence, and to all Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Scott. May I now turn to the Defence. May first, before turning to the Defence, I inquire whether the statement that the Chamber decided to ask for production is ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour. We'll just put them together. It's my understanding from the questions by counsel for the appellant that he referred to a statement of 1996. Is that correct, Mr. Hayman, that's the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe it's the last day of May and the first day of June, 1996, a statement taken in London by three investigators from your office, and I have their names if it's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure I found the statement that you were asking, so I wanted to confirm. Yes, we have copies of the statement for Your Honour. I'll just hand them to a member from the registry. I've just provided the statement of Mr. Watkins dated the 31st of May, 1996, and the 1st of June, 1996, to the Bench, to the registry, and a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. copy to counsel for the appellant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I suggest -- may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What I suggest is I'm going to ask some of my colleagues to look at this while I proceed with my examination, and if at the end of my examination there's a need to have the witness review part of the statement and comment on it, I'll try and do that at the end, but in the interim, I would ask for your full attention while we proceed. I understand this is -- this is a lengthy statement, but I don't -- I'm not suggesting we break and that I read it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: It's fine, Mr. Hayman. You can proceed like that. We appreciate your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Hayman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, you were shown a lot of documents, and some of them I'll try and get them back in front of you; others, given the time limitation it's not going to be possible to put them all on the ELMO and go one by one. So I want to start with one of the last documents that you saw and perhaps you remember it. It was a report. It is Exhibit 456/32 from the trial. And it's a report from Colonel Blaskic to the Supreme Command, May 7th, 1993. And there's a paragraph at the end that says: "Command and control function properly and all missions proceed," et cetera. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, and it seemed to contradict the one before it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier in that document you were shown a statement by the author of the document, referencing a problem in Fojnica. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of the incident in Fojnica where a -- the commander of the HVO forces in Fojnica refused an order to engage BH army forces by Colonel Blaskic, simply refused, simply: No, we're not going to do that. Have you heard of that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that doesn't ring a bell, unless that was the detail within that Fojnica, but it was the confusion that was mentioned in that Fojnica which I thought was interesting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's in evidence in this case so we won't belabour it, but suffice to say that if there was a rebellion by the battalion or whatever the formation was in Fojnica, they refused to carry out the orders of Colonel Blaskic, should one conclude that command and control were functioning properly as stated in the conclusory paragraph of this document, or should one look at the underlying events and understand what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour. This is completely argumentative and leading. We're back on redirect, not cross-examination, and it's not up to counsel to argue with the witness or argue his case. I object to that. Also, the document is clear on its face. It says except for Fojnica. It's very clear. There's no suggestion to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question for the witness is: If the "except for," the unit in Fojnica is acting in a rogue manner, what does that tell us about command and control generally in this army or militia, whatever you want to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again it's a mischaracterisation to generalise on that when the specific document is talking about one area, one incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can the witness please be allowed to comment? I only have a few minutes, and I don't want to yield too much of that time to Mr. Scott. Could the witness comment on the fact that in Fojnica, the -- there was a revolt by the HVO unit there? And what does that tell us? What should that instruct us with respect to the actual situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would tell me two things. One, he had communications, otherwise he wouldn't have known about that chaos but it was clear he would not be able to command and control that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that -- strike that. Now, you were shown a number of other documents that referenced communications between the Central Bosnia operative zone headquarters and the Kiseljak HVO concerning Gomionica and military activity in the Kiseljak region around the 17th and 18th of April, 1993. Do you recall those? I'd like you to look at two documents quickly. They are Exhibits 141 from the first Rule 115 motion and 142 from the first Rule 115 motion. And perhaps you can look at them while they're put on the ELMO so that the Court can also follow along. You're looking now at the first order. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 19 April 1993 at 0835 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 0600 hours. Oh, sorry. I see, yeah. Above. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to give the Court some perspective -- well, 19th of April, you weren't there, so I will withdraw that. Do you see paragraph 1, "occupy Gomionica, the crest of the hill above the village"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why would that -- why would a military commander direct his forces to the hill above a village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It gives one tactical advantage in fields of fire, to control access entry into the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the high ground typically of greater military significance and strategic importance than the low areas below, even if they're built-up areas with the civilian population or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically speaking, yes. Tactical there, rather than strategic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if you could look at the second document that I gave you. This is a reply document, informing the Central Bosnian operative zone of what happened, what happened with respect to your order that we take the hill above Gomionica. Do you see in paragraph 1, first of all, they state: We haven't been able to take full control of Gomionica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if you go down to the second bullet, do you see the statement: "During the preparations for this operation, for the purposes of safeguarding the operation, we had to forcibly disarm the villages of Visnjica and Rotilj, where we lost quite a lot of our force and time." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an order -- was there anything in the prior order you saw that told the HVO Kiseljak to go into Visnjica and to go into Rotilj and disarm villagers and otherwise engage in conflict with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does this witness know? Can we have some foundation? Do we have the prior order in front of us in terms of whether this witness knows the history of the orders, all the orders issued at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Counsel can argue that until he's blue in the face at the end of the case, but for now I've shown the witness two documents and I'm asking him a succinct, clearly stated question regarding those two documents and I would like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the earlier documents you saw and this one, was there anything in the first document that directed the HVO Kiseljak to go into Visnjica or Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but they might have been between where the forces were and the crest of the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can represent to you that Rotilj is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I ought to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- south-west of Kiseljak, Gomionica is to the north of Kiseljak. They're in opposite directions from Kiseljak. And there are maps in evidence in this case, so the Court can refer to them if necessary. But would you agree there's nothing in the order directing these forces to go into Visnjica or Gomionica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yet they report back: Although we weren't able to carry out the task you gave us, we did do some other things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what does this tell us, what should this tell us about whether there was command and control by Colonel Blaskic over what the HVO Kiseljak was doing, even at the times, the very times, that there were, according to the war diary, which is Exhibit 2 to the second Rule 115 motion, there were communications between those two -- communications that counsel pointed out in his cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it proves to me there was issuing of order, a response and failure to carry out the exact task and it seems to suggest they did some other things that were not required in the first half. So there is, to me, an element there of independence of the unit to do what it thought it should be doing. It didn't directly interpret that order. Or it did, but it seemed to do additional things as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I note for the Court that my client was charged and convicted of crimes in Visnjica and Rotilj in this case. Now, Mr. Watkins, you were asked whether Dario Kordic exercised control over Tihomir Blaskic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to elaborate on your answer. To your knowledge, did or could Dario Kordic give a military order to Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he could. How welcome that would be, I don't know, but yes, I believe he could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if Tihomir Blaskic gave a military order to his subordinates that Dario Kordic didn't agree with, what do you think would happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kordic would intervene, either counter the order or use forces which we believe were associated with him to carry out what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say forces associated with him what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We discussed earlier the Jokers, which was a unit which was closely connected and our belief came under the personal control of Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to go to PA15, and I think we will need the document as our -- all of our collective recollections are not sufficient to call up these mental images in our minds. Thank you. This is an order concerning the passage of UN vehicles. Do you see in paragraph 1 that the order is directed to the issue of entry of UN vehicles and "military formations" into the area of combat activities? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a problem in any way, if you have ongoing combat in an area and elements from the international community want to go into that area, even though they are not prepared to, for example, defend themselves or they're not capable of being protected against harm from the ongoing combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are circumstances in which that would be undesirable and counter to what a military commander might wish to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed, the international element, could it not, could come and go to the tactical advantage at least of one side or the other, by causing a cessation of hostilities, giving one side the time to undertake some manoeuvre or action that it otherwise might not be able to undertake? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. We acted as a sort of -- we always tried to get entry to where there was combat but clearly in trying to do so that could advantage or disadvantage one commander or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you offer any other insight into why Colonel Blaskic might have a concern about the entry and egress of United Nations Warriors carrying UN personnel in an area where combat was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are we engaging in speculation, Mr. President? This witness wasn't even on the ground at the time of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed him the order, Your Honour. I didn't. He chose the subject matter, and I think I should be allowed to explore it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry could you ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was: Was the role are of, for example, BritBat with their Warriors, did that become an issue of concern or contention that might be useful background for the Court with respect to this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There would be times and particularly by the time I got up there in May/June, where in fact the initiative was in the hands of the Armija forces and one saw a characterisation of defence and -- of the HVO, and attacking by ABiH. And one would reference to Travnik and Bugojno and other areas. Now, when that happened, we wanted to get in to see what was happening and also to try and calm things. Now, that -- in that particular time when I was there would be not to the advantage of the Armija forces to have us wandering around in their area of operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now Exhibit PA51. If it's handy I'd like to put it on the ELMO. If not, I can pose a question without doing so. This is a communication again to Kiseljak by Colonel Blaskic, saying, among other things: Justify my orders as a response to provocations of the other side. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see take the most favourable possible and always justify my orders in response -- yes, I do. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does any superior commander want their subordinates to respect and defend and justify the orders from the superior commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One wouldn't expect in a Western army for it to be questioned. It was to be carried out. It wouldn't require a response or a comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, in a Western army this order would be unnecessary, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 would be unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you surprised by paragraph 2 or do you think that's normal, that's understood in at least a Western army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be taken as -- yeah, it would be understood. It wouldn't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to see PA56. I'm going to also need the B/C/S version, which on my copy is on the back, but it probably is a separate document in the Court's files. Do you see on the English version the third paragraph has been interlineated through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the paragraph that talks about we need -- if there are these deaths, we need to present them differently --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if you look at the B/C/S version. Do you see it's been crossed through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it's the same document, yeah, it's been crossed through. I'm afraid my language isn't good enough. Yeah, it's crossed through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So someone didn't agree with paragraph 3; is that correct? Is that the appearance of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Someone didn't agree or the author decided to take it out. It clearly wasn't required by someone, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I could ask the interpreters for a translation of the B/C/S phrase to the left. Ovo ne.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you were shown also Exhibit 456/109, which were minute notes from a meeting that involved a very large number of people. Can you see that, please, 456/109? And while we're gathering that, perhaps 112 as well, 456/112. This is a long document. I'm simply going to ask that you go back to the last page, the third paragraph from the end. And first, I want to note, the signatories on this, the signatories are all political figures; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And three paragraphs from the bottom, there's a reference to: "The military are requested to do something in order to avoid a conflict of jurisdiction between the military and the civilian government." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beginning: "The Ministry of Defence of the HZ HB"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, would it be normal in a situation as existed in 1993 in the Vitez pocket for there to be an attempt to coordinate military and civilian authorities with respect to issues such as this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to rephrase that question, or state it again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I just ask the author of this? I can see the signatures at the bottom. Who is it going to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We would need to look at the first page for that - if the first page could please be put on the ELMO - which states: "Excerpt of the minutes of a meeting".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. It's strange in that one would expect those jurisdictions to be clear. We're talking about -- there would be clear differences between who was in control of civilian affairs and who is in control of military affairs. But in a confused situation, one can imagine that some jurisdictions do get blurred, so they might have been seeking clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it appear that in September of 1992 there was a need to deal with that issue from these minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would appear to be, yes, absolutely. Although I wasn't there in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understood. If now we could go to the same notebook, 456, but Exhibit 112. You were also shown this document. If you look at the third paragraph of this document, is this a request for a joint meeting with the 3rd Corps by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You were asked about -- actually, you were told by Mr. Scott that the Kiseljak pocket was not cut off from the Vitez-Busovaca pocket until sometime after the conflict erupted on April 16th, 1993. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me find a document. I may need a moment, and I'm going to ask you to comment on it. The document is PA75, one of the Prosecutor's rebuttal documents. If it could be put on the ELMO, and I can frame it in the meantime. It's a report dated February 10, 1993, from the Kiseljak Brigade, from the operations and training organ, to the Central Bosnia operative zone command, titled "Report on the course of events in the -- in a particular place, Klokoti and Bilalovac area. Now, rather than take the time to read the entire thing, I'd like Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you to turn it over to the back, please, the second page. And about ten lines down, there's a sentence that begins: "On 27 January". Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says there was an action, and then on down about six lines below. No. Please. Keep that up there. We need to keep it on the ELMO. Does the Court already have a copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I'm just reminded that the document is still a confidential one, so it shouldn't be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's not my information, Your Honour. Perhaps the Prosecutor can comment. It is PA75. And quite frankly, from looking at it, there's no reason it should be confidential, but perhaps the Prosecutor can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think we can provide much assistance. I apologise for that. But on the face of the document, there's no particular indication of why it would be confidential, unless it had -- revealed the identity of some particular witness, I guess is no longer, or certainly not at the moment, here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Fine. So let's deal with it as public, as not confidential. Please, you can put it on the ELMO, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are a couple of sentences I want to draw your attention to, and I'm sorry, I can't point to it. There's a sentence towards the middle of the portion that's visible that begins "the units of the Muslim forces." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The units of the Muslim force set up a checkpoint in the village of Bilalovac." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then down another six or seven lines, there's a sentence that begins: "After finding out that a part of the Kiseljak-Bilalovac road has been cut off"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can represent to you it's very clear in the record of this case that the Busovaca-Kiseljak road was cut off on or about the 27th of January, 1993, and was never reopened during the relevant time period for this case. I don't think I have a further question on that issue, Your Honours. I simply didn't want it left unaddressed. You were asked about the military police, and you mentioned the name Marinko. Were you thinking of Marinko Palavra?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. He took over from Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he replace Pasko Ljubicic at some time in the late summer or early fall 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been late summer. Yes, I was there at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware that was at Colonel Blaskic's initiative, that he requested that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were rumours. I didn't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've had a chance to quickly look at the statement and there's just one passage I'd like brought to the attention of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Before you refer to the statement, Mr. Hayman, do you want to admit this statement into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And then, Madam Registrar, can you give a number to this document for purposes of reference.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be numbered Exhibit H1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Fine. You may proceed, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not numbered, but I think we should show the witness the first page so that he can orient himself with respect to the document, and perhaps the last, to see what the date is and that he signed it. And then I'm going to direct his attention to a particular passage. Actually, I notice that the copy the witness has is different from the copy that we were given. The copy the witness has appears to have a face page, with perhaps identifying information of who took the statement and that kind of thing. We don't -- oh, no, we have it. We have it on one copy, Your Honour. I'm sorry. Mr. Watkins, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have a recollection of meeting with Mr. Spork and a second gentleman indicated on the first page, on or about late May or early June 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this the two days of interviews that you referred to earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I will count the pages. If you go to the sixth page, they're not numbered other than by the Bates number 78, ending in the digit 78?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, the copy we have is numbered --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Oh, it is, it is. Excuse me. It's page 6. I see that down next to the signature. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm on page 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read the first paragraph and then I'm going to ask you if you can tell the Court what is this about. Is this something you've already testified to or something new?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beginning "I was personally involved..."?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I was personally involved along with Alastair Duncan commander BritBat forces with negotiations to allow the free passage of the convoy. The convoy had initially been given clearance through the pocket by Colonel Blaskic."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will. "The convoy had initially been given clearance through the pocket by Colonel Blaskic, and therefore, it was him to which we initially turned to secure its secure movement. However, the Jokeri stated that they would only accept the authority of Dario Kordic. It was not until the arrival of Dario Kordic at the checkpoint and his personal intervention in the situation that we secured the agreement of the Croat military forces to allow the convoy to reassemble and pass on through the pocket to Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the Convoy of Joy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Convoy of Joy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that paragraph consistent with your recollection of these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you provided this information to the Prosecutor's office in or about the 1st of June, 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I think it's time to have a break now, so we will reconvene in half an hour. And perhaps we will start with questions from the Bench of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please be seated. So we resume the hearing, starting with questions from the Bench of the witness. May I ask my colleagues -- Judge Guney first. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, what is your assessment about the appellant's effective control, or lack of effective control, over HVO units in Central Bosnia? This is the first question. And the second one is: Are you aware of any lack of animus toward the Muslim -- the animus of the appellant toward the Muslim population of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just ask -- should I be seeing this on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My assessment of the control or lack of it of the HVO in Central Bosnia is that certainly on paper we would see very clear lines of connection between operational zone commander, Tihomir Blaskic, and all of his brigade commanders. But because of the physical isolation, which I have discussed before, that created enormous difficulties in terms of command and control, and communications indeed would be difficult. One I thing that I have yet to mention, but I think is important, is also to understand the level of training and capability of the HVO units which I witnessed, not just the HVO, but the ABiH forces, were largely consisting of rather irregular groupings formed into brigades, but largely of untrained soldiers - this is certainly the case in the HVO - but commanded, usually, by an officer that had some JNA experience. So I don't believe, and I didn't see, the command and control which I would expect in a Western army, and I can explain that in terms of the geographical isolation and the level of training, even where they were collocated in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket of a direct chain from Tihomir Blaskic to the man at the barrier or in a trench. In terms of your second question, Your Honour, can I just confirm, by "lack of animus towards the Muslims" that you mean lack of -- could I just ask for clarification of what exactly you mean by animus?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel, Your Honour, I've given you an incomplete answer. I believe you to mean here: Did the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding general behaviour, did you observe a sort of animosity with regard to the Muslims as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not from Tihomir Blaskic. He was, of course, in conflict with them, but in terms of a philosophy of cleansing an area or of any massacres or genocide, that was never articulated to me by Tihomir Blaskic. It was articulated to me by Anto Valenta and to a slightly lesser level but certainly from Dario Kordic as well, slightly more sophisticated in his terms, but not from General -- or sorry, Colonel, as he was at the time, Blaskic. He always came across as a professional soldier. That indeed is the way that his opponents saw him as well. He was never accused by them, to me, anyway, as being responsible for any war crimes, whereas Dario Kordic was often mentioned as connected with war crimes, but not General Blaskic, Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Weinberg, please. JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: Mr. Watkins, I have one question. You mentioned the Convoy of Joy, which could pass because of the written orders of General Blaskic and the confirmation of Mr. Kordic. You also mentioned the Muslim doctor, I think it's on transcript page 29, of the transcript, the Muslim doctor that was needed at Stari Vitez, and that you asked General Blaskic for authorisation, which was granted after you returned on several occasions. But before that, you mentioned the convoy of the patients which had to return. My question is: If on that occasion you also had consulted with General Blaskic, had a written order, or what was the -- was there any authorisation or discussion previous to the convoy of the patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was -- with regards to the Travnik patients' convoy, we could not have undertaken such a task without consulting both Croat leadership and Muslim leadership, because of the fact we were going to cross a front line. I can't honestly remember the particular negotiations. It could have been Filip Filipovic. They took place in the UN headquarters, at the school near Vitez. But certainly, we had the agreement of both sides that this convoy should be allowed to pass, and specifically with reference to Colonel Blaskic, when I was stopped by that HVO unit at Dolac, they said they did not take orders from Tihomir Blaskic. JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher, please, to put to the witness, and on the ELMO, the second part of document 380B, this interview dated the 16th - I can't read it in B/C/S - in 1993, in any event. And if I may ask the witness to comment on this statement given by Blaskic. What is your assessment? You have discussed the question of investigations ordered by Blaskic previously.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This, Your Honour, is, I believe, the -- it is the document I was shown earlier with regards -- and the explanation was that this was a press interview. I was interested in whether the journalist was actually physically in Central Bosnia, interviewing General Blaskic, or whether there was a physical separation between the questions and the answers. And I was also interested, Your Honour, in the fact that this was a press report, and when you're writing in conditions of war to your population, you have a certain message, and one doesn't give a message of disorder, incoherence, fragile command structures. You would want to give a message of things are going well, yes, they're extremely difficult, but our generals and our soldiers are doing their best. And so I'm not really convinced as to how useful this particular report was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could be kind enough, and Mr. Usher, please, that we can see it in the entirety. What would be your assessment when you read this page until the end? Is it a fair response to allegedly committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just take a moment to read that before responding. I really would not have expected Tihomir Blaskic to have actually said that. The question -- the paragraph at the top discusses "the physical operation is not an essential or decisive factor," and it mentions Kiseljak as we've already spoken, also mentions Sarajevo. And I think the most rudimentary knowledge would indicate that Sarajevo's isolation was -- there were particular and peculiar circumstances there, and one could not credibly argue that its separation from its command structure did not create problems. So I see a journalist answering -- asking some quite loaded questions, and a response which I personally, in my experience in interaction with Blaskic, is not the sort of response he would have given. I hope, Your Honour, I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Having been part of the ECMM, this observer mission, did you come across this incident yourself? Did you yourself discuss the incident mentioned there with the appellant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This incident in Ahmici actually happened while I was in Gornji Vakuf, and I arrived some one month after this. I don't remember discussing it with Tihomir Blaskic. I do remember discussing it with Ivo Santic and Pero Skopljak, but not with Tihomir Blaskic, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And when you discussed it already, were there ongoing investigations about the crime allegedly committed in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were certainly ongoing investigations by the international community, and my immediate -- person to whom I reported was Jean-Pierre Thebault, who was very personally involved, visited the site, and was very active in explaining to the international community what he saw, and his understanding of what went on. And certainly we talk -- it mentions here about staged and skillfully shown to foreign reporters. I mean, it's not credible. There was an atrocity there. It was witnessed by the international community. They reported what they saw. They didn't skillfully in any way make propaganda out of this. They simply reported what they saw. And in my experience, this is not the words of Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one final question. Just by chance having been for that long a period of time in the area, did you ever hear the word "ciscenje" by one of the political or military leaders in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That particular word, Your Honour, does not -- I do not recognise that word. I may have heard a translation of what that means, but I don't recognise that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you hear, maybe in the French language, a translation to that end that it would mean, "nettoyer le terrain"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you have demonstrated my weakness in languages. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. I only wanted to ask you whether by chance you came across this term alluded to in several documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I do not recognise the word "ciscenje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I would put a couple of questions to the witness myself. The first refers to the meetings, frequent meetings, you had with Colonel Blaskic at the time you referred to them. What I would like to know: If in conversations during these meetings it ever happened that Mr. Blaskic related to you of any difficulty he had in preventing activities, criminal activities, as the case may be, by the Jokers or other groups, or to punish the perpetrators. Did he ever mention any of these incidents to you in your conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. He didn't mention difficulties. I'm not entirely surprised about that. His professional demeanour would not really encourage him to tell me, particularly as I had military experience myself, of difficulties within his command. Although there are a number, two instances that I can think of, one referred to earlier, with Ivica Rajic, where he did state that he was having difficulty in enforcing, and another one where it wasn't Tihomir Blaskic himself, but it was a member of his staff who told me that there were difficulties with Cerkez, and this is when we wanted to gain entry to the village of Kruscica over the water issue which I mentioned earlier. So Tihomir Blaskic is not the sort of person that was indiscreet. When we wanted some depth and some rumour, Your Honour, we would speak to those with looser tongues and probably less aware of the sensitivities. I simply got straightforward military responses from Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. The second question I wanted to ask you is how far you are aware, or which is your knowledge, of the military situation in Kiseljak in April and June 1993. You may not have been there, but you -- exactly on the spot, but you have known exactly what was the situation between the different groups combatting against each other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was there by June, but not there in April. We had seen a number of attempts, certainly in Herzegovina, for the Croatian forces to take territory. We saw activity in Mostar, we saw activity towards Jablanica. We saw a lot of Croatian activity in the Prozor area. And this activity demonstrated a desire of the HVO to take Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. forces. By the time -- sorry -- to take ground. By the time that I was in Central Bosnia, the situation was different, and in Central Bosnia, unlike in Herzegovina, the Croatian community was on the defensive. We had -- we were always trying to defuse tensions, to create confidence through joint commissions, but we could see that the tensions were getting greater. Some of this we believed was to do with wanting to take territory, or hold territory, in accordance with what was going on at an international level and the control of cantons that were being discussed. But in Central Bosnia, we saw - and I was personally involved with in May, June, and right through October - a Croatian community that was in difficulty in Central Bosnia. There is no doubt about the circumstances that were very hard. And it was the Armija forces at that stage who were in the offensive posture. So we had seen, for instance, the defeat of the HVO in Zenica. We saw the Travnicka Brigade, and I witnessed the HVO presence in Travnik when I first arrived. We had our joint commission structure there. But the Travnicka Brigade, under Jozo Leutar was effectively annihilated. When I say annihilated, I mean as a formed unit not that every individual was annihilated. We also saw activity then spread to other areas. We saw Kakanj, and again the Croat population on the defensive and also in Bugojno. So we -- that is my understanding of the situation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I was specifically interested in Kiseljak. You referred specifically to end of May/June. Is your knowledge that the situation was the same in April, from what you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I -- Your Honour, from what I understand, certainly in the case of the change from any -- to a defensive posture was middle of April through the period. And I'm sorry I didn't more specifically address in the earlier question your interest in Kiseljak. I did state earlier that I wasn't entirely sure when the Kiseljak pocket was separated from the Vitez-Busovaca pocket, but we later heard that that was as early as January. And certainly January there had been a flash of activity, certainly in Gornji Vakuf area, and also, I understand, in Central Bosnia, where Croat forces and Muslim forces who had been working together and fighting against the Serbian forces started to fight each other. And it was at that moment that we set up these Busovaca joint commission and I was involved in setting up the Gornji Vakuf joint commission, and this was the attempt to separate forces and to quieten. And we did so successfully until April when we saw the new outbreak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Just to follow on that: The situation you now are referring, referred to about Kiseljak, was the same in Busovaca in April, or was it a different situation, from what you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I know, the situation in April was the same as I witnessed in May and June. The pockets were separate. The ability to move from one pocket, from Vitez and Busovaca to Kiseljak had effectively ended by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: More than the pockets, I was referring to this defensive attitude or offensive attitude, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the defensive attitude of the Croats had already -- was in evidence in April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I don't have further questions to put to the witness. Judge Schomburg, you have an additional question. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Just to come back to the question of the state of mind shown by the appellant at that time. May I ask you, maybe I have confused the time you have been there in the area. May I ask you: Did you attend a press conference 27th of April, 1993, where, inter alia, Kordic, Kostroman, and Valenta were present? Did you ever hear that the appellant expressed remorse, anger, or annoyance about what happened prior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't at that press conference, but I do know that there were conferences held on a regular basis, and we heard earlier of those that included the appellant. Although I note that you didn't mention the appellant in that particular meeting, or maybe I haven't quite read that properly. In terms of answering your second part of the question, Your Honour, did I ever hear the appellant express remorse, anger or annoyance about what was happening, what had happened prior to that and I assume you mean Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Ahmici, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't honestly say that I do remember him expressing remorse specifically about Ahmici, but to give you a full answer about his posture and attitude, motivation with regards to the humanitarian situation and conduct of activity, I only can report that he was not motivated by any philosophical ambitions. He simply dealt with the military situation on the ground. And I was asked earlier on cross-examination about this one brain, two bodies, which I felt was incomplete, and in fact I think worse than that, because it doesn't give -- it's the easy answer. We had two leaders in the same pocket acting on behalf of the Croatian community, but it doesn't allow for the different motives and motivations behind those individuals and what they were doing. And history is littered with examples of people who are wearing the same uniform, who are carrying out the same actions, but, for completely different reasons. One can think of the Great War. Did every commander in the Russian army believe in the same things as Stalin? No. Would it be right to characterise somebody like Field Marshall Rommel as having the same instincts, motivation as his political masters? I think not. It would be an injustice to characterise Rommel in that way. I don't want to make any direct comparisons with the appellant, but the principle is the same, that he wore the same uniform; he was doing what he thought was right for the Croat community, but not with the same motivations, as I believe were evinced by, demonstrated by the political leadership that I saw there in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Well, this concludes the examination of this witness. We thank you for your cooperation, Mr. Watkins, and you are excused now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I see both the Prosecution, the Defence maybe -- Mr. Farrell, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There is one issue that was -- excuse me to Judge Guney. I apologise, Your Honour. There was one issue that was raised in one answer I gave or one comment on the record that I wanted to clarify. The one issue that was raised was that in the testimony of the witness who just left, the use of the disclosure, the timing of the disclosure of the witness's statement by the Prosecution or as indicated by my friend the lack of disclosure of the 1996 statement was put to the witness as part of his evidence, which the appellant clarified was for his Rule 68 argument. That was not, as far as I understand, part of his additional evidence for which he was to be called, but I appreciate that my learned colleague was given the opportunity to address that. What's now on the record, according to the submissions of my learned colleague, was that it appears that you can draw the inference, according to them, from the refusal of the Prosecution to provide this witness with his statement reflects in the fact that the Prosecution was suppressing exculpatory evidence. We'll certainly make submissions on that next week, on what inferences you can draw. The only thing I wanted to comment on was that if this is the evidentiary basis upon which this argument will be relied upon, that the Prosecution wants to address in evidentiary form the allegation that it specifically and deliberately refused to provide this individual with his statement. The policy of the OTP in 1996 was not to provide any witnesses with any statements at that time because there was a concern then about the witness's handing around their statements primarily in the former Yugoslavia. I spoke with the investigator, and he's in a position to put a declaration in to that effect that this had nothing to do with this individual witness or the inability to provide him with his statement, that it was a policy of the OTP at the time because of other circumstances that had arisen. This witness was informed of that very reason in 1996 when his statement was given and according to the investigator he indicated that he understood. He then subsequently --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I put this and present it in declaration form if the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Why didn't you raise this question in cross-examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Because it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You could have put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: In terms of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Whether he understood whether he had said that he understood that was the practice of the Prosecution, there were reasons for that. You could ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That might have been the fault of the Prosecution and for that, I apologise. But it was only afterwards at the break that I was able to find out what happened in 1996 by trying to contact with the people who had spoken to him. I wasn't in any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Farrell. You could ask for the floor when the witness was here, and something. I mean, I would have accepted that you put an additional question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Then that's my mistake. I thought I wouldn't raise it while he was still here. I'm certainly willing to raise it with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Because he could clarify the matter immediately if he understood that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Of course. And if that's the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now you're asking to put additional evidence on that. It could have been clarified orally immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, it could, but the discussion about what the policy was and what the motivation was of the Prosecution for withholding evidence back then and not providing it to the witness could not be answered by this witness. That -- you're right, Your Honour, with respect to the part of the evidence you've indicated, but for the rest of it, as whether you could draw the inference as to what the practice was of the Prosecution at that time could not come from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You may be aware in any case of the practice of the Prosecution in this Tribunal, so this is not a big problem. But the fact that you are putting now is that the witness, the witness, was aware that -- of that practice. This is the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: This could have been asked the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's fine, then. That's a concern of the Court, then that's fine. The second issue that I wanted to raise was that when the Defence counsel -- sorry, before I go on to the next issue, on the issue about the inference to be drawn from the failure to give the witness the statement, if that's an issue which remains on the record then it's an issue which the Prosecution may seek leave to address something that this witness couldn't have spoken to. The second issue -- sorry. Proceed. Thanks. The second issue is a comment I made on the record indicating when Mr. Paley had indicated, as I recall, that the witnesses was not provided a copy I indicated -- I spoke after Mr. Paley and indicated that was incorrect. I just wanted to clarify that. That was my mistake. I thought he was speaking about whether or not this witness was -- had asked for his statement for this hearing. And this witness was contacted and never requested the witness statement for the purpose of this hearing. I was not intending to refer to what eventually Mr. Hayman clarified as a previous time. So I just wanted to make that clear, that obviously I'm in no position to refute what the witness said in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would just note that if indeed that's the policy of the Office of the Prosecutor not to give witness statement and they can show that to us and it's an issue we can enter into an oral stipulation and it won't be an issue. I think the real issue, though, is that the Defence was never given this statement. The Defence was never given the information about Kordic controlling the Jokers. It's not a question of the witness getting it. It's why weren't we given this information? Why weren't we given this statement despite the obvious relevance that this would have had to our case and that's not an issue for today. If they have something additional they want to tender, fine. But that's the real question. And certainly we are arguing in this case and it's in our brief and we're going to argue it in final argument that it's a very, very serious problem, procedurally and substantively in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I have no problem with the Defence being able to argue this point of law and raising it in their brief. I would agree with Mr. -- with counsel for the appellant that it actually isn't an issue for today and that's the reason why I objected that it was put through a witness, but in terms of the argument we'll respond to it next week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank both parties. Now we understand which is the basis for the arguing of the Defence. This question being clarified, we can move to start the examination of the following witness. I'd like to propose the following: Not to split in two portions, over two days, the consideration of the next witness. We might proceed the examination-in-chief before the break now and meet again -- Mr. Hayman, will that require a full hour or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There are four possible witnesses remaining, Your Honour. One of them, depending on the testimony of this witness, we may decide it's cumulative or duplicative and we will not need to call that fourth witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: It's not my question. Is whether the examination-in-chief of this witness will require the full hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of the remaining witnesses this is the most substantive, most important witness. I think it may require more than one hour. The other two who we are certain we will call will be fairly short witnesses. So what I'm assuring the Court of is we can finish all the evidence by Thursday as planned. We will not need Monday. But the next witness is a witness who was very involved in many events and so he's going to be the longest of the three remaining witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I understand that. So we start examination-in-chief, we'll see whether we can conclude it. I hope so. And then decide whether we meet again in the afternoon, in the early afternoon, to conclude the consideration of the witness, or whether we put it to tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So can we call the witness. Of course, that will be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While that's being done, Your Honour, I've been asked to clarify one thing in the documents that we cited in this last witness. I apparently referred to the war diary as Exhibit 2 to the second Rule 115 motion and in fact it is Exhibit 14. So I needed to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
